Functions of the middle ear

In shortThe middle ear transmits, amplifies, protects and equalizes pressure for sound reaching the inner ear.

  • Transmission: vibrations pass from the tympanic membrane through the ossicles to the oval window, which contacts the perilymph of the scala vestibuli.
  • Sound pressure magnification (22 times): the ossicular lever system gives about 1.3 times, and the large tympanic membrane area concentrated on the small oval window gives about 17 times (1.3 × 17 = 22).
  • The tensor tympani pulls the handle of the malleus inward, keeping the membrane continuously tense for optimum vibration.
  • Impedance matching: overcomes the inertia of the perilymph by converting low-density air waves into movement of the high-density aqueous inner ear medium.
  • The round window (secondary tympanic membrane) is flexible, connects to the scala tympani and moves with the basilar membrane to absorb perilymph waves. Its fixation causes hearing loss.

Acoustic (tympanic) reflex

Loud high-pitched sounds cause reflex contraction of two muscles that protect the inner ear.

Tensor tympani

  • Pulls on the tympanic membrane
  • Makes it more tense
  • Prevents vigorous vibration

Stapedius

  • Prevents inward displacement of the stapes in the oval window
  • Prevents damage to cochlear structure
Clinical relevance

The reflex fails if the loud sound is extremely sudden (gun shots, jet planes) because of the total reflex time and muscle latent period, causing serious irreversible inner ear damage.

Eustachian tube and pressure equalization

  • Connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx so both sides of the tympanic membrane face atmospheric pressure. It is normally collapsed and opens during swallowing, yawning or chewing.
  • Adults: curved course prevents drinks entering the middle ear. Children: more horizontal and wider, so breast feeding while the baby lies flat may let milk reach the middle ear and cause severe infection.
  • Air travel: pressure in the middle ear is relatively higher on ascent and lower on descent, so continuous swallowing or chewing gum is needed. If the traveler is asleep or the tube is obstructed (common cold), drum rupture may occur.
  • Continuously patent tube: the person's own voice radiates to the ear. Continuously obstructed tube: air is absorbed, the drum is sucked inward, causing pain and deafness.

Inner ear and the cochlea

The inner ear lies in the petrous temporal bone, the strongest bone weight for weight. It is a fluid-filled cavity, unlike the air-filled middle and external ears. Its hair cells are mechanoreceptors for hearing and equilibrium. The bony labyrinth and membranous labyrinth are separated by perilymph; the membranous labyrinth contains endolymph, which never connects with perilymph. The membranous labyrinth has an auditory part (cochlea) and a non-auditory part (equilibrium).

The cochlea is a coiled tube 35 mm long. The basilar membrane and Reissner's membrane divide it into three scalae.

ScalaFluidRelations
Scala vestibuli (upper)PerilymphCommunicates with scala tympani at the apex; ends at the oval window (stapes footplate)
Scala tympani (lower)PerilymphEnds at the round window (secondary tympanic membrane)
Scala mediaEndolymphContinuous with the membranous labyrinth; does not communicate with the other scalae

Organ of Corti

It lies on the basilar membrane, has a spiral shape from apex to base, and contains the hair cells (auditory receptors). Their processes pierce the reticular lamina, supported by the rods of Corti. The tips of the hair cells are embedded in the viscous, elastic tectorial membrane. Each cochlea has 20,000 outer and 3500 inner hair cells, in four rows: three rows of outer cells lateral to the tunnel of Corti and one row of inner cells medial to it.

Inner hair cells

  • 3500 cells, one row
  • Receive 90-95% of afferent neurons

Outer hair cells

  • 20,000 cells, 3 rows
  • Receive only 5-10% of afferent neurons; each neuron supplies several cells
  • Most efferent fibers (cholinergic, from the superior olive) end here and hyperpolarize them

Afferent cell bodies lie in the spiral ganglion in the modiolus. Their axons form the cochlear division of the vestibulocochlear nerve and end in the dorsal and ventral cochlear nuclei of the medulla oblongata. Each auditory nerve has about 28,000 afferent and efferent fibers.

High-yield

Tight junctions between hair cells and adjacent phalangeal cells keep endolymph away from the hair cell bases. The basilar membrane is relatively permeable to perilymph of the scala tympani, so the tunnel of Corti and the hair cell bases are bathed in perilymph while their processes are bathed in endolymph. This is essential for generating the receptor potential.

Mechanism of hearing

  1. Collection and conduction

    The pinna collects sound and determines its direction. Waves pass down the external auditory tube to the tympanic membrane, and the ossicles magnify the vibrations.

  2. Oval window and perilymph

    The oval window moves forward and backward, moving the perilymph of the scala vestibuli and Reissner's membrane up and down.

  3. Basilar membrane vibration

    The endolymph of the scala media vibrates and so does the basilar membrane, moving the hair cells.

  4. Shearing

    The tectorial and basilar membranes are both attached to the limbus and slide on each other, bending the stereocilia back and forth.

  5. Depolarization or hyperpolarization

    Organ of Corti moves up: stereocilia bend away from the limbus (modiolus), K+ channels open and K+ influx depolarizes the cell. It moves down: stereocilia bend toward the limbus, K+ channels close, causing hyperpolarization.

  6. Transmitter release

    Depolarization lets Ca2+ enter, releasing transmitter that stimulates the afferent auditory fibers (about 90% around inner hair cells, 10% around outer).

Electrical responses of the cochlea

Endolymph

  • Resembles intracellular fluid; secreted by the stria vascularis
  • Rich in K+ (135 mEq/L), poor in Na+ (15 mEq/L)
  • +80 mV relative to perilymph

Perilymph

  • Resembles extracellular fluid; formed from plasma by diffusion
  • Rich in Na+, poor in K+; 0 mV
  • Communicates with CSF by the prelymphatic duct

The endocochlear potential (+80 mV) needs energy from the metabolic activity of the stria vascularis and is abolished by severe hypoxia or cyanide poisoning. Hair cells are -70 mV inside relative to perilymph, giving about 150 mV across to the endolymph. The tunnel of Corti is filled with perilymph because endolymph has nearly the same ionic composition as axoplasm, which would prevent nerve impulse transmission.

Cochlear microphonics

  • Potential variations in the endocochlear potential caused by up and down movement of the basilar membrane; they start in the hair cells.
  • Increase with frequency and amplitude of sound, have no latent period, and disappear in severe hypoxia of hair cells.
  • Recorded by an electrode on the cochlea and an indifferent electrode on the neck; best at the basal turn.
Don't confuse

Cochlear microphonics are not related to the action potential in the auditory nerve.

Discrimination of sound

The cochlea detects 20 to 20,000 Hz; higher frequencies are ultrasonic and not detected. Maximum sensitivity is around 1000 to 4000 Hz, matching the optimum sensitivity of the ear drum and ossicles.

Place (Helmholtz) theory

  • Resonance of about 20,000 transverse basilar fibers of differing thickness and tension
  • Short, tense fibers near the base vibrate to high frequencies
  • Long, lax fibers near the apex vibrate to low frequencies
  • Different hair cell groups reach different auditory cortex localities

Traveling wave (Von Bekesy)

  • Modification of the place theory
  • Stapes footplate produces traveling waves in the scala vestibuli, base toward apex
  • High frequencies peak near the base; low frequencies near the apex
  • Basilar membrane is readily depressed, and the site of maximal distortion depends on frequency
Intensity (loudness)
Larger basilar membrane portion vibrates, more action potentials
Locality
Near sounds seem stronger; direction by time difference between the two ears
Sound patterns
Cortical function; two sounds separated if interval exceeds 1/10 second

Vestibular apparatus: otolith organs

The vestibular apparatus detects equilibrium. The non-auditory labyrinth contains the utricle and saccule (two sacs in the bony vestibule) and three semicircular canals, with perilymph around and endolymph inside.

Each macula (otolith organ) is a ridge of columnar epithelium with hair cells bearing 50-70 stereocilia and one large kinocilium, covered by gelatinous material holding calcium carbonate otoliths (otoconia). In the erect head the utricle macula is horizontal and the saccule macula vertical.

Bend toward kinocilium
Depolarization
Vestibular nerve discharge

Bending to the opposite side hyperpolarizes the hair cells and inhibits afferent impulses. Each hair group faces a different direction, so each head position is detected by a particular group.

Functions of the maculae

  • Static equilibrium: right and left utricle impulses balance in the erect position; tilting displaces otoliths by gravity and the unbalanced discharge gives the sensation of tilt.
  • Linear acceleration: on sudden forward acceleration the otoconia (greater inertia) are displaced backward, causing a false sensation of falling backward and automatic forward leaning.
  • Receptors for postural reflexes (labyrinthine statotonic and righting reflexes).
  • Orientation under deep water, where visual and proprioceptive impulses are absent; a person with inner ear disease who closes his eyes may sink.

Vestibular apparatus: semicircular canals

There are three canals on each side in three planes at right angles. Each has an ampulla opening into the utricle; the anterior and posterior canals share one opening, so there are five openings. The ampulla contains the crista ampullaris: hair cells (40-70 stereocilia and one kinocilium) embedded in a gelatinous cupula. The canals detect angular acceleration (rotation) in the plane of the canal. Hair cells depolarize when stereocilia bend toward the kinocilium; in horizontal canals the kinocilia face the utricle, in vertical canals the opposite.

Rotation to the right

  1. Start

    Endolymph rotates to the left by inertia, bending both cristae left. The right crista (toward the utricle) is stimulated, the left is inhibited, giving the sensation of rotation to the right.

  2. After 20-30 seconds

    Inertia is overcome, endolymph moves with the canal, the cupula returns by elasticity and the sensation disappears.

  3. Stoppage

    Endolymph momentum keeps it moving right, stimulating the left crista and causing a false sensation of rotation to the left (vertigo). It fades after 20-30 seconds.

The canals are stimulated at the beginning and end of rotation and on change in rate, not at constant rate. They also have a predictive function against mal-equilibrium. Stimulation methods: angular or linear acceleration, electrical stimulation on the mastoid process, and thermal (hot or cold ear wash moving the endolymph).

Results of stimulation

Vertigo
False sensation of counter rotation after stopping
Nystagmus
Slow component opposite to rotation (from canals); rapid component in the direction of rotation (from brain stem reticular formation); fixes objects in the visual field
Autonomic reactions
Nausea, vomiting, bradycardia, hypotension, sweating, pallor
Past-pointing (Barany)
After rotation to the right, the person touches to the right of the target
Muscle tone
Increased on the same side, decreased on the opposite side

Vestibular connections and clinical points

Afferents travel in the vestibular division of the 8th nerve to the vestibular ganglion (Scarpa's, first order neuron), then to the vestibular nuclei (second order neurons) in the medulla and lower pons.

Vestibulospinal tracts
Facilitate tone, especially antigravity muscles; adjust posture
Medial longitudinal bundle
Links nuclei of nerves 3, 4 and 6; pathway of nystagmus and head and eye righting reflexes
Vestibulo-reticular
Autonomic reactions such as vomiting and bradycardia
Vestibulo-cerebellar
To flocculonodular lobe via inferior cerebellar peduncle
Vestibular nucleus
Inferior cerebellar peduncle
Flocculonodular lobe
Dentate nucleus
Superior cerebellar peduncle
Opposite thalamus
Superior temporal gyrus

This is the vertigo pathway; a second route runs from the vestibular nucleus through the reticular formation to the opposite thalamus and temporal gyrus.

Clinical relevance

Meniere's disease: raised endolymph pressure of unknown cause, with attacks of vertigo, nystagmus, vomiting, loss of equilibrium, tinnitus or defective hearing; severe cases need surgical removal of the vestibular nerve. Vestibular nerve section: vision is clear only with the head fixed, ocular fixation is lost and walking is difficult.

Postural reflexes

Gravity, disturbance of the body's center during movement and support on two limbs require redistribution of muscle tone through postural (equilibrium) reflexes. Receptors are in proprioceptors (especially antigravity muscles), the labyrinth and the retina. Their basic mechanism is the stretch reflex, and a center of equilibrium lies in each temporal lobe near the auditory center; unequal impulses to the two centers trigger the reflexes.

Check yourself

How is the 22-fold middle ear pressure gain obtained?

Ossicular lever (about 1.3) multiplied by the tympanic membrane to oval window area ratio (about 17).

Which side's crista is stimulated at the start of rotation to the right?

The right crista, which bends toward the utricle; the left is inhibited.

Why does the tunnel of Corti contain perilymph?

Endolymph has nearly the same ionic composition as axoplasm, which would prevent nerve impulse transmission.

Key Points / Quick Review

Middle ear

  • 22 times gain (1.3 lever × 17 area)
  • Acoustic reflex: tensor tympani and stapedius; fails with very sudden sounds
  • Eustachian tube equalizes pressure

Cochlea

  • Scala vestibuli and tympani: perilymph; scala media: endolymph
  • Inner hair cells receive 90-95% of afferents
  • Endocochlear potential +80 mV; hair cells -70 mV
  • Stereocilia away from limbus: K+ influx, depolarization

Frequency

  • High frequencies at base, low at apex
  • Range 20-20,000 Hz; best 1000-4000 Hz

Vestibular

  • Maculae: static equilibrium and linear acceleration
  • Canals: angular acceleration; vertigo, nystagmus, autonomic reactions
  • Meniere's disease: raised endolymph pressure
